# $Z$-sight: Unifying Vision-Language-Action and Latent World Modeling

First public date: 2026-11-18.

Authors: Junjie Ye, Yiqi Zhao, Muchen Xu, Celina Shiyu Wang, Hao Dong, Ruohai Ge, Rong Xue, Benjamin J Kolligs et al.

Classification: 2026 · Embodied context (live auto-indexed preprint).

## Abstract & key idea

We introduce $Z$-sight, a unified robot foundation model that couples vision-language-action (VLA) and generative latent world modeling. Video-based world action models (WAMs) show the value of joint future-and-action generation for control, yet inherit the heavy cost of video generators. Recent latent-space policies avoid pixel generation, yet typically align intermediate features or rely on frozen target encoders, decoupling future prediction from the VLM's native feature space. $Z$-sight instead predicts the future directly in the visual token space in which its VLM perceives the present. Coupling a foresight expert and a continuous action expert with the VLM in a mixture-of-transformers, $Z$-sight jointly denoises future spatial tokens and actions at inference without pixel reconstruction or external encoders. Trained on human video and robot trajectories, $Z$-sight achieves 81.9% success on SIMPLE (+9.6 points over the strongest baseline) and 73.3% across six Unitree G1 tasks (+20.0 points) at 110 ms per chunk, while remaining competitive on tabletop benchmarks.

# NereidVLA: Learning to Understand and Navigate the Underwater World

First public date: 2026-11-18.

Authors: Chenjie Zhao, Zhiliang Zhu, Quan Chen, Yuquan Xue, Xingxue Shi, Puyue Wang, Zhiqiang Zhao, Kangye Zheng et al.

Classification: 2026 · Embodied context (live auto-indexed preprint).

## Abstract & key idea

Underwater navigation requires translating visual spatial cues into motion, yet marine vision-language datasets rarely include paired robot trajectories. We present NereidVLA, a vision-language-action model that transfers marine spatial knowledge to language-conditioned 3D navigation. We first train Sea2Know on approximately two million marine examples to learn target grounding, spatial relations, and scene structure without paired robot-motion supervision. We then adapt it using expert trajectories executed under simulated underwater vehicle dynamics. Given RGB histories and a language instruction, NereidVLA predicts discrete motion tokens that decode into local 3D trajectories for closed-loop tracking. Evaluation combines an independent six-dimensional underwater navigation understanding benchmark with offline prediction and closed-loop navigation. Under matched navigation training and execution settings, marine spatial pretraining increases simulation success from 72.4% to 84.4%. Without fine-tuning on the real test environment, NereidVLA achieves 78.75% success in laboratory-pool robot trials, compared with 47.50% for InternVLA-N1. These results show that marine spatial supervision can support downstream motion learning and physical underwater navigation.

# DiWALI: Diffusion Policy Learning in World Models via Latent Action Inference from Human and Robot Play

First public date: 2026-11-18.

Authors: Akshay L Chandra, Iman Nematollahi, Lingyue Zhao, Daria Kulikova, Angela P. Schoellig, Fabien Despinoy, Abhinav Valada.

Classification: 2026 · Embodied RL (live auto-indexed preprint).

## Abstract & key idea

Learning robot manipulation is constrained by the availability of action-labeled robot data, for both imitation and world models. Humans can demonstrate skills in seconds, but their demonstrations lack the required robot actions. We introduce DiWALI, a framework that learns and improves diffusion policies within a world model trained on human and robot play. DiWALI infers latent actions from consecutive frames using an inverse dynamics model, enabling world model training without action labels, and grounds them in robot commands through a decoder trained separately on robot play. Skill policies are trained over latent actions from action-free human demonstrations and improved with reinforcement learning in imagination. On the CALVIN benchmark, DiWALI policies trained solely from human demonstrations substantially outperform baselines trained with robot demonstrations. Incorporating human play into the world model training also yields stronger policies after fine-tuning than using the same amount of robot play alone. Experiments on a physical robot show that skills learned primarily from human demonstrations are further improved in imagination with a world model trained on human and robot play. Together, these results demonstrate that human experience can support both manipulation skill acquisition and subsequent policy improvement, reducing reliance on action-labeled robot data. Videos, dataset and code are available at https://diwali.cs.uni-freiburg.de.

# RoboMorpher: Scaling Robot Morphology Representations for Cross-Embodiment Action Prediction

First public date: 2026-11-18.

Authors: Wenwei Lin, Yan Qin, Weiliang Deng, Zixuan Li, Kaixuan Wang, Zanxin Chen, Yue Chen, Tianshuo Yang et al.

Classification: 2026 · Embodied context (live auto-indexed preprint).

## Abstract & key idea

Learning shared action representations is central to cross-embodiment manipulation. However, identical joint values can produce different spatial configurations across robots, limiting representations learned from joint values alone. We introduce RoboMorpher, a morphology-conditioned action tokenizer that jointly reconstructs joint angles and link poses to associate control coordinates with their kinematic effects. MorphGen supplies scalable kinematic supervision by generating serial-arm descriptions from survey-derived geometric priors. We pretrain RoboMorpher on 40 million morphology-state pairs and integrate the frozen tokenizer into a vision-language-action policy for discrete prediction and continuous refinement. We also introduce EmbodiBench, a ten-task benchmark with 30 generated URDFs per task. With downstream URDFs excluded from tokenizer pretraining, the policy achieves 56.40% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and 23.27% on EmbodiBench, exceeding continuous joint-space control by 9.73 and 15.34 percentage points. Removing link-pose supervision reduces EmbodiBench success by 17.94 percentage points, supporting morphology-aware geometric supervision for joint-action representation learning.

# HINT-WAM: Hindsight-Informed Training for World Action Models

First public date: 2026-11-18.

Authors: Phuong Tuan Dat, Qi Li, Xinchao Wang.

Classification: 2026 · Embodied RL (live auto-indexed preprint).

## Abstract & key idea

World action models (WAMs) have shown promising generalization and data efficiency in robot manipulation by coupling action generation with predictions of future visual dynamics. Translating these capabilities into reliable task execution, however, remains a challenge for existing post-training methods. Offline supervised fine-tuning provides dense supervision on expert trajectories, but its flow-matching action expert is trained only on noised demonstration actions and never on the intermediate states produced by its own sampler; task-specific adaptation can also compromise pretrained capabilities. On-policy reinforcement learning trains on the policy's own behavior, yet sparse task rewards make exploration and credit assignment difficult, while dense reward shaping still provides scalar evaluations rather than direct action targets. We introduce HINT-WAM, the first on-policy self-distillation framework that supervises the action expert on its own sampling trajectories using hindsight, the future video of the demonstration, as privileged information available to the WAM itself. For each demonstration observation, the student generates its action through its own denoising trajectory, and at the states along this trajectory the same model acts as a teacher conditioned additionally on this hindsight, providing a conditional action distribution as a dense training target, while the student sees only deployment-time inputs and needs no environmental rewards or simulator interaction. To transfer this supervision to a flow-matching action expert, HINT-WAM distills the teacher into the student with an energy score, a distribution-level objective that matches the teacher's action distribution from the student's own samples rather than regressing its velocity field. The project web is available in https://tuandattt.github.io/hintwam/.

# Depth Before Breadth: Reverse-to-Forward Curriculum with Advantage Decomposition for LLM Agent

First public date: 2026-11-18.

Authors: Siyuan Du, Yuxin Liu, Meng Tang, Haoran Li, Yechao Bai, Feiyang Pan, Jia He.

Classification: 2026 · Agent RL (live auto-indexed preprint).

## Abstract & key idea

Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a common approach for training large language model (LLM) agents on long-horizon tasks. However, learning from sparse terminal rewards makes credit assignment and exploration difficult. We approach these challenges through a policy-induced capability region, the set of states from which the current policy can reliably complete a task. Near its boundary, an agent may need only a few actions to reach a more solvable state, even when the goal remains distant. This reduces long-horizon learning to two coupled subproblems of reaching that state and completing the task from there. We address them with paired advantages and a progressive reverse-to-forward curriculum. The advantages provide separate signals for reaching more solvable states and completing the task from them, while the curriculum expands the capability region backward along successful reference trajectories and then into off-reference states through on-policy exploration. On ALFWorld and WebShop, our method outperforms competitive agentic RL methods at both model scales, achieving success rates of 90.1%/96.1% and 80.2%/82.6% with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct, respectively.

# DrawScore: Evaluating Generated CAD Models against Engineering Drawings

First public date: 2026-11-18.

Authors: Haorui Chen, Shiteng Lu, Zhanyu Guo, Zaixi Li, Yunhe Ni, Yaosong Du, Yichen Xiang, Xiande Huang et al.

Classification: 2026 · Core & World RL (live auto-indexed preprint).

## Abstract & key idea

Automatic CAD generation is commonly evaluated with volumetric IoU, Chamfer Distance, and surface F-score, which barely penalize local errors that occupy only a small fraction of a part's volume or surface area, such as a misplaced hole or a slot on the wrong face, even though such errors are critical to manufacturing. We formalize these metrics in a unified integral form and show that the weight of a local error decays as the (k+q)-th power of its size, where k is the dimension of the integration domain and q is determined by the penalty function. Guided by this analysis, we propose DrawScore, which projects both models into three orthographic views with visible and hidden lines, as in engineering drawings, and applies a saturating penalty along the projected curves, so that the weight of a local error decays only linearly. Controlled experiments confirm the predicted decay orders, and on outputs of existing CAD generation agents, DrawScore exposes errors in outputs that IoU rates as nearly perfect. DrawScore further improves generation as a reinforcement learning reward and, for CAD generation from engineering drawings, serves as a test-time verifier without 3D ground truth or an additional reward model. Our code is available at https://github.com/UESTC-Simon/DrawScore.

Keywords: reinforcement learning reward, test-time verifier, reward model.

# Self-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Better-Structured Medical Explanations in Small Language Models

First public date: 2026-11-18.

Authors: Prakhar Mishra, Bhavya Yajush Awasthi, Tanuja, Nishant.

Classification: 2026 · Core & World RL (live auto-indexed preprint).

## Abstract & key idea

Small language models (SLMs) can run on commodity hardware and support privacy-preserving, on-premises clinical deployment, but their medical explanations are often short and poorly structured compared with large language models. Recent supervised approaches such as Meerkat transfer chain-of-thought reasoning into 7B-8B backbones, yet their training objective does not directly target the style or organization of the generated rationales. Building on the instruction-tuned Mistral-7B backbone, we investigate whether a lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) step can improve explanation structure without human preference labels.We apply Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with LoRA adaptation to 2,000 Meerkat-derived medical prompts, guided by a simple self-supervised reward that favors longer, lexically diverse, and well-punctuated responses while penalizing very short ones. Training for about 170 PPO steps on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU yields a stable increase in the average reward. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons show that the RL-tuned model produces longer, more organized, multi-point explanations while preserving the underlying medical content.We discuss the promise and the limitations of self-rewarded RL for shaping the style of medical explanations.

# SHAPE: Discrete Supervision and Parallel Continuous Streams for Learning Dexterous Manipulation from Egocentric Human Data

First public date: 2026-11-18.

Authors: Yaping Li, Zhihong Liu, Jiacheng Li, Yi Yang, Wenchao Yue, Mingzhe Ye, Xiangcheng Liu, Yiyang Chen et al.

Classification: 2026 · Embodied context (live auto-indexed preprint).

## Abstract & key idea

Egocentric human recordings are far cheaper than dexterous robot demonstrations, promising stronger pretraining and direct skill learning without task-specific robot data. Yet humans and robots differ in morphology and kinematics, so human recordings lack the joint positions and actuator commands that supervise robot policies, providing only retargeted end-effector (EEF) actions. This raises two questions: how human data should supervise the policy, and how a dexterous robot should read out actions at deployment. We address both in SHAPE (Supervision from Human Action tokens with Parallel Executable streams), a vision-language-action (VLA) model whose backbone predicts discrete action tokens of EEF chunks as an auxiliary task, while a shared flow-matching expert outputs two executable streams, EEF and joint. On a bimanual robot with 22-DoF hands, a matched study shows that discrete supervision helps learn from human data, driving backbone gradients and shaping action-informative representations across domains. Under standard control pipelines at deployment, direct joint readout excels at fine-grained control with robot demonstrations, scoring 0.80 across six tasks against 0.63 for π0.5, whereas IK-based EEF readout excels at human-to-robot transfer. Pretrained with human data and discrete tokens, SHAPE learns new tasks from human demonstrations without task-specific robot data.

# RECLAIM: Robot-Vision-Informed Adversarial Patch Defense via Embodied Attention Feedback

First public date: 2026-11-18.

Authors: Jiayou Zhu, Peng Guo, Litian Zhang, Xinze Shi, Yuting Zhang, Zelong Yu, Yize Tian, Jirong Liu et al.

Classification: 2026 · Embodied context (live auto-indexed preprint).

## Abstract & key idea

Vision-language-action policies control embodied agents through a perception-action loop grounded in physical interaction, where adversarial patches can corrupt action predictions and thereby alter subsequent observations. To mitigate these threats, many existing defenses rely on policy adaptation or auxiliary models, but require additional training or inference. We introduce RECLAIM, a training-free, inference-time defense that uses a frozen VLA's own attention response to local visual interventions to guide purification during closed-loop embodied manipulation. Our key insight is that attention changes induced by local edits provide feedback for choosing where and how to purify as the robot interacts with its environment. RECLAIM combines this feedback with robot geometry to refine patch localization and select local treatments, then revalidates them as the agent's embodied actions change the observed scene. We evaluate RECLAIM against patches generated by four adversarial attack methods across multiple manipulation task suites under frozen VLA control. Under adversarial patch attacks, RECLAIM succeeds in at least one rollout on 95% of the evaluated tasks and raises rollout success on LIBERO-Object from 0% without defense to 70.0%. Its mean decision time is only 548.9 ms per control step. These results highlight policy-guided visual purification as an effective approach to defending embodied agents against adversarial patches and recovering closed-loop task execution.

# Cooperative UAV and Ground Station for Robust MEC of Dynamic Aquatic IoT: A Generative AI-Enhanced Approach

First public date: 2026-11-18.

Authors: Jiahao You, Ziye Jia, Chao Dong, Qihui Wu, Zhu Han.

Classification: 2026 · Embodied RL (live auto-indexed preprint).

## Abstract & key idea

The increasing aquatic Internet of Things (AIoTs) require computational support and coverage in applications such as maritime search and rescue. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can offer low-cost, flexible aerial services, and ground stations (GSs) can provide powerful supports, which can cooperate to help the AIoTs in complex scenarios. However, the collaboration between UAVs and GSs for AIoTs faces challenges of task uncertainties, AIoTs trajectory uncertainties, heterogeneities, and limited computational resources. To address these issues, we propose a cooperative UAV and GS based robust multi-access edge computing (MEC) framework to assist AIoTs in completing computational tasks. Specifically, we formulate the optimization problem of joint task offloading and UAV trajectory to minimize the total execution time, which is in the form of mixed integer nonlinear programming and NP-hard to tackle. Therefore, we propose the algorithm of generative artificial intelligence-enhanced heterogeneous agent proximal policy optimization (GAI-HAPPO). The proposed algorithm integrates GAI models to enhance the actor network ability to model complex environments and extract high-level features, thereby allowing the algorithm to predict uncertainties and adapt to dynamic conditions. Additionally, GAI stabilizes the critic network, addressing the instability of multi-agent reinforcement learning approaches. Finally, extensive simulations demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms the existing benchmark methods, thus highlighting the potentials in tackling intricate, cross-domain issues in the considered scenarios.

# Homeward: No Place Like the Training View

First public date: 2026-11-18.

Authors: Mingyang Lyu, Yinqian Sun, Gongce Cao, Guobin Shen, Yuhao Zhang, Lu Jia, Chenfei Yan, Qian Zhang et al.

Classification: 2026 · Embodied context (live auto-indexed preprint).

## Abstract & key idea

Vision-language-action (VLA) policies implicitly assume that third-person cameras remain fixed at their data-collection poses; once a camera is bumped, remounted, or swapped at deployment, task success degrades precipitously even though the underlying task and robot remain unchanged. We present Homeward, a training-free, plug-and-play observation adapter that canonicalizes observations from an uncalibrated deployment camera back into the training view for frozen VLA policies. Our design stems from a closed-loop diagnostic paradox in simulation: while re-rendering perturbed views into the training camera with oracle geometry recovers much of the lost performance, substituting an off-the-shelf feed-forward 3D foundation model can leave the policy worse off than applying no correction at all. This degradation concentrates on the thin, articulated robot arm, which feed-forward depth prediction tears and scatters - yet the arm's exact 3D state is already known from robot kinematics. Homeward exploits this asymmetry: it estimates what is unknown - camera parameters and static scene depth - from the live RGB frame and a single training-view reference, and renders what is known - the moving robot links - directly from the kinematic model. Evaluated across $\sim$300,000 closed-loop episodes spanning four frozen VLAs, Homeward boosts success across all 1,599 camera variants of LIBERO-Plus from 62.5%, 76.5%, 68.0%, and 3.6% to 77.6%, 95.1%, 91.2%, and 26.4% for OpenVLA-OFT, $π_{0.5}$, $π_0$, and OpenVLA, respectively. Without any scene fine-tuning or deployment camera calibration, Homeward extends to 6-DoF random placements, focal-length changes, and, with per-step pose estimation, continuous intra-episode camera drift, while matching or surpassing a calibrated, scene-trained view-synthesis baseline on three of four policies on LIBERO-Plus.

# PIPETTE: Prompt Injection Purple-Teaming for Robust LLM Agents

First public date: 2026-11-18.

Authors: Lipeng He, Yihan Wang, Jiawen Zhang, N. Asokan.

Classification: 2026 · Agent RL (live auto-indexed preprint).

## Abstract & key idea

Large language model (LLM) agents routinely interact with untrusted external data, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks that hijack agents into executing attacker-chosen tasks. ## Abstract & key idea

This paper presents a framework for computer-aided music composition and performance based on quantum reinforcement learning and multi-agent interaction. We introduce the agentic orchestra, where musical agents evolve distinct mindsets through trial-and-error engagement with a musical environment, rather than through training on large datasets. The agents are implemented as parameterised quantum circuits. They evolve distinct compositional behaviours, referred to as mindsets. This enables the exploration of musical decision spaces using quantum superposition and entanglement within a hybrid quantum-classical loop. We present two complementary agent architectures: atomistic agents, which process pitch and rhythm independently, and holistic agents, which handle pitch and duration as unified note events. Mindsets are shaped through musically grounded reward functions, which can be combined and weighted to develop different mindsets across agents. The resulting system positions quantum computing agents less as autonomous composers and more as adaptive musical partners, each developing its own musical personality through interaction rather than imitation. Demonstrations show how agents generalise their learned behaviour to previously unseen material, operating in interactive and offline batch modes using MIDI-encoded music. While quantum computers are still in development, experiments conducted on IBM quantum hardware confirmed that musically meaningful learning is achievable with existing quantum computers. For composers and performers, the agentic orchestra opens new possibilities for emergent, process-oriented musical creativity, offering a scalable foundation for quantum computer-aided music composition as quantum computing technology continues to advance.

A key challenge is linking changing egocentric perception with spatial evidence anchored to stable locations for long-range navigation. We propose CityNav-VLA, a dual-frame vision-language-action model for urban navigation integrating dynamic egocentric context with persistent allocentric spatial memory. The UAV incrementally accumulates visual observations on a fixed north-up map initialized with geographic and landmark priors, preserving evidence across viewpoint changes. A dynamic query conditioned on the instruction, current observations, UAV state, and motion history retrieves relevant memory evidence to predict a map-frame target. Cumulative ablations show that navigation-map features yield the largest gains, while metric coordinates further improve endpoint accuracy. We introduce Divergence-based Uncertainty-aware Adaptive Action Chunking (DUAC), a post-hoc method that extracts trajectory-conditioned predictive uncertainty from the vector field of a pretrained VLA. First public date: 2026-11-18.

Authors: Paul König, Sascha Marton, Stefan Lüdtke, Christian Bartelt.

Classification: 2026 · Embodied RL (live auto-indexed preprint).

## Abstract & key idea

Safe reinforcement learning (RL) aims to prevent agents from taking actions that are dangerous or destructive to their environment. This is especially important for safety-critical domains, such as robotics or autonomous driving. Formal verification can be used to prove agent safety through safety constraints. However, in practice, many policies do violate safety constraints, and thus are verified to be unsafe. Since the goal is to obtain a safe policy, we would need to retrain a new policy from scratch and then verify it again until a candidate happens to pass. Both training and verification are usually not cheap, which makes this process inefficient. We introduce VESPA ($\textbf{VE}$rifiable $\textbf{S}$ymbolic $\textbf{P}$olicy $\textbf{A}$daptation), a framework for targeted fine-tuning of decision tree policies. We show that using counterexamples for policy adaptation can make existing unsafe policies safe, or at least make considerable progress towards safety. Targeted fine-tuning of the existing policy on those counterexamples enables it to learn how to avoid violating safety constraints. We thus use the result of a formal verification as a training signal for fine-tuning. On CartPole, VESPA raises the mean number of verified safe steps from 63.8 to at least 92.7, reaching after two iterations what the same loop without counterexamples reaches after ten. On MountainCarContinuous, VESPA turns an unsafe policy into a safe policy in 53 of 60 runs. We conclude that counterexamples from a verifier are an effective training signal, which can be utilized to systematically improve the safety of policies. In this paper, we present AeroRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework in which an aerial navigation policy iteratively learns from its own failures. Judged in this way, its sampled actions and even rule-based proposals that hurt it when imitated directly become reliable supervision. Moreover, an episode terminates at its first failure, concealing subsequent failures until the earlier ones are repaired. AeroRSI thus renews its supervision in every round, anchoring the failures of the current policy, verifying repairs by its continuation, and distilling them while keeping its behavior elsewhere. # Replay, Don't Resample: Off-Policy Consolidation of Long-Horizon RL Experts

First public date: 2026-11-18.

Authors: Zhenrui Yue, Gongxiaohui Chen, Huimin Zeng, Honglei Zhuang, Jiashuo Sun, Zhen Han, Dong Wang.

## Abstract & key idea

Frontier post-training follows a common recipe: train one expert per domain with reinforcement learning (RL), then consolidate the experts into one model via multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). Such consolidation is expensive: the student samples in every environment again, an expert scores every sampled token, and the student inherits the drift of the final experts. Yet we argue that the experts' RL runs have already produced what consolidation needs: rollouts with their sampling probabilities and rewards, in the order the experts learned from them. We propose multi-expert replay policy distillation (MRPD), which replays these training logs through the student in the experts' order. At each step, the policy gradient is recomputed on these scored trajectories, and the final experts' distributions are distilled at the logged prefixes. Following the experts' own trajectory reduces the training-inference mismatch and keeps the student within the clip range, so the replay is off-policy in origin but quasi-on-policy throughout consolidation. MRPD samples nothing and calls no environment or reward model: the trainer is the sole process, and consolidating the experts costs only about a seventh of the compute used to train them. On three long-horizon agentic domains (reasoning, search and SQL), MRPD yields the best student model, substantially outperforming online RL baselines, and surpassing MOPD from the same experts at a fraction of MOPD's cost. Our analysis on the same logs shows that the replayed trajectories carry most of the gain, and that both the policy gradient and the distillation term add to it. Most interestingly, the order of the logs matters more than their amount or rewards, suggesting that expert training logs are a curriculum, not a data mixture.

# GTI: Grounding Task Intent Throughout Long-Horizon VLA Manipulation

First public date: 2026-11-18.

Authors: Tianqi Gong, Haochen Niu, Yusheng Zhao, Lantao Zhang, Haoyu Liu, Rendong Ying, Peilin Liu.

Classification: 2026 · Embodied context (live auto-indexed preprint).

## Abstract & key idea

Vision-language-action (VLA) models generate local actions from visual observations, language, and robot state, but long-horizon manipulation requires the global task intent to remain grounded in the currently executable context. We propose GTI (Grounding Task Intent), which uses the current observation and execution history to localize the active subtask and its execution phase. For the same local subtask, GTI generates two phase-dependent visual targets: an interaction/contact state and a local completion state. The local language instruction and the corresponding phase-specific visual target jointly condition the VLA, specifying both what to do now and what state should be reached at the current phase. During execution, anomaly monitoring and local recovery re-establish an intent-consistent execution context through rollback, re-observation, and phase re-evaluation after persistent deviation. We evaluate GTI on RoboCasa365, VLA-Arena Horizon-Long, and real-world PiPER tasks. Relative to matched Global-FT baselines, GR00T success on seen composite RoboCasa365 tasks increases from 14.6%/12.1% to 31.8%/20.4% under ID/OOD evaluation. On VLA-Arena, GTI+$π_{0.5}$ reaches 47.6% overall success versus 45.2% for an adapted ForeAct baseline, with gains of 5.2/6.0 percentage points on the harder L1/L2 tasks. In the three real-robot task experiments, mean full-task success increases from 21.7% to 59.2%. The results indicate that persistent semantic intent localization and phase-conditioned visual grounding improve multi-stage execution, while failure-triggered local recovery provides additional deployment-time support.

# CoSlice: Coordinated Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for 5G Network Slicing Allocation

First public date: 2026-11-18.

Authors: Pengxin Wang, Nakjung Choi, Jingdi Chen.

Classification: 2026 · Agent RL (live auto-indexed preprint).

## Abstract & key idea

Radio Access Network (RAN) slicing is a shared resource allocation problem: each slice seeks to satisfy its Service Level Agreement (SLA) with minimal radio-resource consumption, while all slices compete for a limited resource budget. This creates both an intra-slice trade-off between SLA assurance and resource efficiency and an inter-slice conflict over shared resources, calling for specialized yet coordinated control. In this work, we present CoSlice, a coordinated multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for inter-slice physical resource block allocation in Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN). CoSlice uses preference-conditioned slice agents for fast resource allocation and an LLM-based coordinator to adapt their objectives using global network observations at a slower timescale. We formulate the problem as a multi-objective partially observable stochastic game (mo-POSG), establish the existence of a Preference Correlated Equilibrium, and derive a sublinear regret bound for the learning procedure. We implement the algorithm by using a two-stage training procedure that consists of multi-objective pretraining and joint optimization. We build a network slicing evaluation environment using ORANSlice and its radio-frequency simulator (RFsim), supporting realistic protocol-stack execution and application traffic across multiple slices. Experimental results show that CoSlice reduces both average and tail SLA violations compared with other centralized and multi-agent baselines under diverse slice workloads.

# Navigating Robots from Unknown and Uncalibrated Exocentric Cameras via Map Estimation

First public date: 2026-11-18.

Authors: Raul Steinmetz, Raphael Druon, Yusuke Yoshiyasu, Akihisa Ohya, Ayanori Yorozu.

Classification: 2026 · Embodied RL (live auto-indexed preprint).

## Abstract & key idea

Exocentric cameras, mounted on walls or ceilings in indoor environments, offer wider vantage points and are less easily occluded than robot-mounted cameras, making them an appealing alternative for perception in robot navigation algorithms. Previous methods that use such cameras, however, require their pose and intrinsics to be known before deployment, demanding calibration that is time-consuming, requires specialized personnel, and must be repeated whenever a camera moves or a new room is navigated. We propose Robot-centric Obstacle Maps from Unknown and uncalibrated eXocentric cameras (ROMUX), an agent that navigates a robot toward point goals while avoiding obstacles using exocentric cameras that are both uncalibrated, meaning the system does not require their pose or intrinsic information as input, and unknown, meaning it is not fit to a specific camera during training and does not require pre-deployment fine-tuning. We train a cross-view transformer on large-scale simulation data to predict metric robot-centric obstacle maps from exocentric images, without conditioning image tokens on camera information. A small policy trained with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) then navigates on the predicted maps toward a goal coordinate relative to the robot. We benchmark our agent in simulation with cameras randomized per episode, and it matches the success rates of a PPO policy that navigates from a robot-mounted camera. Further, ROMUX works with one camera or multiple cameras with partial views and has been transferred zero-shot to a real robot using a camera at varying positions and orientations across various room layouts.

Instead of burdening the VLA policies with long-horizon reasoning, memory, action generation, progress tracking, and error recovery, we argue for leveraging their short-horizon manipulation capabilities within an execution-aware framework. We preserve the underlying VLA policy entirely, requiring no additional fine-tuning. Experiments on RoboCasa365 and CALVIN benchmarks show an improvement of 21.9% and 10.4% in success rate over the next strongest baseline. ## Abstract & key idea

In martial arts games, opponent motions must not only be physically plausible but also exhibit appropriate technique, timing, transitions, and target-directed intent. Traditional game animations often rely on handcrafted clips, state machine transitions, and procedural adjustments, which can be labor-intensive and may limit the behavioral diversity of non-player characters. The prototype combines policy-generated motion clips with lightweight state-based control to support interactive opponent behavior. Together, these findings support the feasibility of using a learned martial arts skill repertoire as a motion foundation for animating opponents in VR sparring games.

# Evidence-Based Credit Assignment for Search-Augmented Language Models

First public date: 2026-11-18.

Authors: Wen Wang, Jindong Wang, Jiahua Bao, Tu Yongsiqi, Yihao Liu, Junwei He, Wenkui Fan.

## Abstract & key idea

Reinforcement learning from terminal answer rewards enables search-augmented language models to interleave reasoning and retrieval without step-level annotations, yet outcome supervision assigns identical credit to every search in a trajectory regardless of whether it retrieved useful information. This limitation is especially severe when all sampled rollouts for a question fail, collapsing group-centered outcome advantages to zero even when trajectories gather markedly different evidence. We present Evidence-based Credit Assignment (ECA), which augments terminal outcome rewards with a training-only auxiliary signal measuring how retrieved documents improve the likelihood of a reference answer. Rather than scoring the full dialogue prefix, ECA queries a frozen snapshot of the current policy under an evidence-only prompt containing solely the question and the deduplicated documents observed so far, isolating the utility of retrieved passages from surface variations in generated thoughts or search queries. Within this framework, we compare two return formulations, ECA-Step (which accumulates step-clipped potential increments) and ECA-Horizon (which preserves the telescoping horizon gain in potential), paired with cross-fold group normalization, novelty gating, and search-local token assignment. Across seven Search QA benchmarks, ECA-Horizon improves strict macro exact match over an outcome-only GRPO baseline by 1.03 and 4.80 percentage points on Qwen2.5-3B- and 7B-Instruct, respectively, outperforming both RLOO and GiGPO. # PReMind: When Personal Memory Meets Visual Hazards

First public date: 2026-11-18.

Classification: 2026 · Core & World RL (live auto-indexed preprint).

## Abstract & key idea

Personalized vision-language assistants use visual observations and personal memories to provide advice tailored to the user. When the observed scene contains a physical hazard, personal context, such as allergies, medical conditions, or mobility constraints, can change what help is appropriate. Responding appropriately therefore requires recognizing the visible hazard and applying the relevant person's information. We introduce PReMind-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that evaluates this combination across diverse hazards and personal-memory conditions. It separately measures memory access, grounding, abstention, and hazard response, and assesses joint success on interdependency cases. Existing models often satisfy one requirement while failing the other, and training only for safety or personalization leaves a gap in joint success. We therefore propose PReMind, a two-phase reinforcement learning framework that combines on-demand and forced-call interactions (memory always retrieved) to jointly train grounded memory use and hazard response. At 4B, PReMind raises joint success from 12.9% to 28.6% over its base on the interdependency set and improves hazard adequacy and correct abstention on the main test. Joint-success gains persist under forced-call evaluation and under a second LLM judge across three Phase II seeds; averaged over these seeds, joint success also improves on unseen hazard groups. These findings highlight the need to evaluate and train personal assistants to connect visual evidence with the relevant person's context.

Existing adversarial attacks on VLA-controlled robots mainly optimize prediction-level discrepancies or rollout-level deviations to disrupt manipulation. However, they rarely account for the fact that VLA-predicted commands are not executed directly, but must be realized through downstream control and robot embodiment. Vision-Language-Action models have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities. In this work, we study how to best adapt VLAs to dexterous hands by pairing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL). Consequently, we recommend an adaptation recipe that freezes the VLM, fully trains the action expert, and eschews SFT rollout success as a checkpoint selection metric.

# Option-GRPO: Hierarchical RL Against AI Slop in Code Generation for Unseen SDKs

First public date: 2026-11-17.

Authors: Prashank Kadam.

Classification: 2026 · Core & World RL (live auto-indexed preprint).

## Abstract & key idea

Large language models increasingly produce AI slop in generated code: verbose, redundant, non-idiomatic implementations that pass functional checks but bloat codebases. The problem compounds on SDKs released after the model's training cutoff, where the model has neither idiomatic priors nor compositional understanding. We present Option-GRPO, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that adapts a code LLM to an unseen SDK from its source code alone, without human-written usage examples or test cases, and that explicitly optimizes for both functional correctness and code elegance. Our key insight is that SDK source code contains compositional structure that defines a hierarchy of reusable code patterns (code options) which simultaneously serve as the building blocks of a curriculum and the action space for efficient policy optimization. We show that code options induce a valid semi-Markov decision process, give conditional bounds under which shorter option description length implies more concise and, in expectation, more API-efficient programs, and analyze under stated assumptions how the option hierarchy improves credit assignment by a factor of $\sqrt{T/K}$. Using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with execution-based rewards at each curriculum level, Option-GRPO discovers SDK idioms, composes them into patterns, and assembles patterns into complete programs. Experiments on 12 unseen SDKs with a 32B-parameter base model demonstrate 61.4% pass@1, outperforming flat GRPO by 8.7 points, ExploraCoder by 11.2 points, and ReCode by 6.3 points. Option-GRPO produces solutions that use 34.7% fewer API calls and are 27% shorter than flat-GRPO outputs while maintaining higher correctness, directly attacking the slop problem.
